# Application Performance Workshop Examples

A group of projects used as part of the Application Performance Workshop.

## Prerequisites

The examples included in this workshop require the following.

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)
- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

## JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Download the latest version of JMC from
   [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

2. Specify the version of Java

   When having multiple versions of Java installed, you may need to specify
   which one to be used by JMC. This can be done through the `jmc.ini` file,
   found under the `Eclipse` directory of where JMC is installed.

   Add the `-vm` option followed by the path to the `bin` directory, as shown
   next.

   ```
   ...
   -vm
   /Users/aattard/.sdkman/candidates/java/current/bin
   ...
   ```

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded
   for brevity.

## Examples

The examples explore application performance at three levels: requests across
services, runtime behaviour within a Java application, and the cost of a
specific implementation. Use distributed traces to follow requests, JFR and JMC
to investigate application behaviour, and JMH to compare focused pieces of code
under controlled benchmark conditions.

### Whole Application (multiple JVMs)

Follow a request across components running in separate JVMs to understand how
downstream calls and database operations contribute to its response time.

1. [OpenTelemetry](./opentelemetry/README.md): Trace requests between the Cart
   and Catalogue services and inspect service calls and database queries in
   Jaeger.

### Single Component (single JVM)

Record and inspect a single Java component within one JVM with JFR and JMC.
These examples cover recording setup and analysis tools, then use evidence to
investigate CPU usage, waiting, allocation, memory retention, and exceptions.

1. [Start JFR](./start-jfr/README.md): Start recordings through JMC, `jcmd`, JVM
   startup options, or application code, and explore recording through Java
   Management Service.
2. [Continuous Recording](./continuous-recording/README.md): Keep JFR running in
   the background and dump a recording when diagnostic data is needed.
3. [JFR Print](./jfr-print/README.md): Filter recorded events and export their
   data as text, JSON, or XML for command-line analysis.
4. [JFR Metadata](./jfr-metadata/README.md): Inspect event schemas, including
   field definitions, labels, and descriptions, with `jfr metadata`.
5. [JFR Scrub](./jfr-scrub/README.md): Remove events containing sensitive
   properties with `jfr scrub` and compare this with selective removal using the
   JFR consumer API.
6. [JFR Configuration](./jfr-configuration/README.md): Explore the supplied
   recording configurations and create a custom configuration for the events you
   need to observe.
7. [Custom Events](./custom-events/README.md): Add application-specific JFR
   events and correlate domain activity with JVM events while keeping
   instrumentation code readable.
8. [Crypto Events](./crypto-events/README.md): Inspect JFR security events to
   identify deliberately obsolete TLS usage and examine certificate information.
9. [Socket I/O](./socket-io/README.md): Compare recordings with and without
   simulated network delay to identify socket-read waits and their application
   call sites.
10. [Hot Methods](./hot-methods/README.md): Locate expensive collection lookups
    in execution samples and compare the profile after changing the collection
    type.
11. [Latency](./latency/README.md): Investigate contention when multiple threads
    append file contents to a shared list, then refactor to reduce and eliminate
    that contention.
12. [Garbage Collection](./garbage-collection/README.md): Investigate
    unnecessary object creation and its effect on allocation and garbage
    collection.
13. [Memory Leak](./memory-leak/README.md): Use allocation evidence and compiler
    warnings to investigate a memory leak and compare behaviour after correcting
    the implementation.
14. [Thread Churn](./thread-churn/README.md): Compare platform thread starts
    with a bounded executor using JFR and JMC.
15. [Exceptions](./exceptions/README.md): Find exceptions through JFR even when
    the application swallows them without logging or propagating them.

### Implementation

Compare alternative implementations of a small operation with JMH. Interpret the
measurements within the benchmark’s workload and thread configuration before
applying the results to a wider application.

1. [Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH) Concurrency Benchmark](./jmh-concurrency-benchmark/README.md):
   Compare uncontended counter operations implemented with `synchronized`,
   `Lock`, `AtomicInteger`, and `VarHandle`.

## Common commands

- Build all projects

  ```shell
  ./mvnw clean package
  ```

- Run a goal on a specific project

  ```
  ./mvnw <goal> [<goal>*] --projects <project> [<args>*]
  ```

  Example

  ```shell
  ./mvnw test --projects 'latency'
  ```

- Update the dependencies and plugins

  ```shell
  mkdir -p './target'
  ./mvnw versions:display-plugin-updates > './target/plugin-updates.txt'
  ./mvnw versions:display-dependency-updates > './target/dependency-updates.txt'
  ```
